Is this a dagger which I see before me. This is Macbeth's soliloquy immediately before murdering King Duncan, in which he confronts a vision of a floating dagger—real or imaginary—as the instrument of regicide.

Macbeth speaks in Act II as he steels himself to carry out the murder his wife has urged upon him. A dagger appears to float before him. He questions whether it is real or a hallucination born of his fevered mind. The opening line captures this ambiguity perfectly: is this a dagger which I see before me, the handle toward my hand? The weapon's ontological status remains uncertain.

Macbeth interprets the dagger as a sign from the witches and fate, validating his resolve to murder. The speech conflates the imaginary dagger with the real bloody deed to come, suggesting that thought and action blur together in guilt. What makes the soliloquy so psychologically penetrating is how it reveals Macbeth's susceptibility to supernatural visions and his willingness to interpret them as justification for what he already desires. He addresses the invisible dagger as his guide, inviting it to lead him to Duncan's chamber. The dagger exemplifies the play's deep concern with perception, reality, and mental disturbance, as Macbeth's ambition and fear warp his grip on what is real.
